name: Au
confidence_why: Scorza 1985, the only first-hand description of Au, puts stress on the first syllable unless that syllable has a central vowel (/ɨ/, /e/), and Scorza's own earlier 1973 typescript, which states the pattern by syllable count (third syllable in four-syllable words, first in three-syllable words, initial or final in two-syllable words), is a rougher early version of the same vowel-conditioned pattern rather than a rival analysis, while Elgh 2023 simply repeats Scorza 1985.

catalog_quote: 0.3.2. Stress. Stress normally occurs on the first syllable of a word, which may have up to four syllables. Some exceptions are noted below: (a) The vowel /ɨ/ is never stressed unless the only vowels in the word are /e/ or another /ɨ/. Examples are: (1) mɨ́tɨk man (2) mɨ́te woman (3) hɨ́ne knife (4) k-ɨ́rɨr he-flees (5) k-ɨsáwɨn he-hides (6) k-átɨp he-talks (b) The vowel /e/ is never stressed unless the only other vowels are /ɨ/ or another /e/. Examples are: (7) népere dog (8) pérpere flying fox (9) k-ewát he-gives (10) k-ekíntɨp he-steals ... [vowel chart, same page:] mid central close unrounded : /ʌ/ symbolised /e/ ... [0.3 Presentation, p.218:] an inventory of Au phonemes is given first, followed by comments on stress (which is predictable)

new_statements.quote: Stress is not contrastive phonemically. It usually occurs on third syllable of a four syllable word, the first syllable on a three syllable word, and alternates from word to word on two syllable words, that is from initial or final depending on the word. Stress is recognized by loudness and high pitch. Tone is not phonemically pertinent, nor is pitch. There do seem to be certain pitch patterns involved in intra-village call messages. [typescript; a handwritten 'SYLLABLE' is written above each 'word' in 'from word to word', i.e. corrected to 'alternates from syllable to syllable on two syllable words'; 'intr-village' is hand-corrected to 'intra-village']

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Au (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule field and there are no existing stress statements, so this source supplies the only primary-source placement statement: stress exists, is non-contrastive, and is placed by a syllable-count pattern (4σ: third; 3σ: first; 2σ: initial or final by word). It does not fit a single fixed-position category. Note that Elgh 2023 (LLM 41, p.39, held by the project) reports 'Au generally has stress on the first syllable of the word (Scorza 1985:219)' from Scorza's later sketch, which is compatible with the 3-syllable rule here but not with the 4-syllable rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic (non-contrastive) and its position depends on the word's syllable count: on the third syllable of four-syllable words (= penult), on the first syllable of three-syllable words (= antepenult), and on either the initial or the final syllable of two-syllable words, varying by word. Stress is cued by loudness and high pitch. No lexical tone and no phonemic pitch; some pitch patterns occur only in intra-village call messages.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Usually' hedges the 3- and 4-syllable rules; two-syllable words are stated to vary between initial and final stress 'depending on the word' (lexically). No examples with stress marks are given in the paper.
new_statements.identity_note: Scorza's Phonemes paper (p.2, Introduction) states that Au has three dialects, East, Central and West, and that 'the following analysis represents the Central dialect', carried out in the village of Tumentonik (Torricelli Mountains south of Aitape, Palei-Wapei group per Laycock); it mentions an earlier unpublished phonological analysis of another dialect by Muriel Salisbury (1965). The Rosetta excerpt names no dialect. Elgh 2023's remark draws on Scorza's later sketch of the same language.

readall_conflicts: The only primary statement opened (Scorza, Phonemes of the Au language, Nov. 1973 revision, sec. 5.3.1, p.16) gives a syllable-count-dependent placement: third syllable of four-syllable words, first syllable of three-syllable words, initial or final on two-syllable words by word, with stress non-contrastive. This sits in tension with the secondhand report in Elgh 2023 (LLM 41, p.39; A general first-syllable rule agrees with the three-syllable rule of 1973 but not with the four-syllable rule; the two Scorza statements would need Scorza 1985 p.219 to be read to settle whether the later sketch simplified or revised the 1973 description. The Rosetta Project excerpt of Scorza 1973 (Sentence structures) is silent, and Scorza 1974 (Au paragraphs and discourses) was not accessible.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page scan we hold of Scorza 1985 p.219 (sec. 0.3.2), vowel chart and p.218 'predictable' remark included. (2) The deciding source is a 1985 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch by the long-term SIL fieldworker; its stress note is brief but explicit, with stress-marked examples showing central-vowel avoidance (mɨ́tɨk vs k-ɨsáwɨn, k-ewát, k-ekíntɨp), which is exactly what the 'weight / full-vs-reduced-vowel, left edge' coding encodes. Nothing later and primary exists: Glottolog's descriptive list is all Scorza 1971-1985, and the only post-1985 linguistic work located (Elgh 2023, LLM 41) cites Scorza 1985:219 for first-syllable stress. (3) downloaded now via the Internet Archive: Scorza's dedicated phonemes ms (1971, rev. Nov 1973). Its sec. 5.3.1 (typed p.16) says stress is non-contrastive, cued by loudness and high pitch, 'usually' on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words, 1

tone.quote: Now that we have considered briefly the typological features of each phylum, we will examine the way that the Torricelli languages differ from features typically expected of the Papuan languages. These appear below and are based upon the features outlined by Wurm, Laycock and Voorhoeve (1975:179-186). ... Trans-New Guinea Phylum Sepik-Ramu Phylum Torricelli Phylum PHONOLOGY ... Phonologically relevant tones: often present rare absent

sources.note: Silent on word stress, accent and tone. It neither restates nor bears on the catalog record (Scorza 1985 p.219: initial stress with /ɨ/,/e/ avoidance, coded weight) or the 1971/1973 'Phonemes' statement held by the project.
